title: Testing distributed systems: Jepsen, TLA+ and simulation
goal: By the end you can say which bugs model checking, deterministic simulation, Jepsen-style testing, property tests and chaos experiments each find and miss, and you have built a seeded simulator that finds a lost write in a replication protocol, replays it exactly, and proves the fix over thousands of runs.

warmup.q: Your CI starts a three-node cluster in Testcontainers, kills the leader, and checks that no acknowledged write is lost. It has passed 500 times. What has it shown?
options: The failover is correct
The failover survives crashes, but not partitions
It survived the timings those 500 runs happened to hit, and none of them could be replayed exactly
Nothing at all: tests can't find distributed bugs
warmup.why: Each run killed the leader at whatever moment the scheduler, the network and the JVM produced, and the dangerous moments (a kill between applying a write and replicating it, a pause just longer than a timeout) may never have come up. Had one failed, you couldn't have rerun that exact timing. The second option claims more than the test says: it tells you nothing about partitions either way. The test is worth keeping. This lesson is about tools that search those timings on purpose.

try.title: Search seeds for the lost write
steps: Run the demo below from the `labs` folder. It runs the lab's naive primary-backup protocol on seed after seed, each with its own message delays and at most one fault, until one run loses an acknowledged write.
Before it prints, predict: will the first failure be a crash, a pause or a cut link? Will replaying the seed give the same trace?
Read the last events. Which message did the damage, and when had it been sent?
try.expect:
```text
Searching seeds 0 to 9,999 for a run where the naive protocol loses an acknowledged write...
seed 4 fails after 576 events. Fault: Cut(at=809, forMs=175)
  at 1013 ms n2 is the primary and holds 19, but write 20 was acknowledged

The last events before it (heartbeats left out):
    949  n1 -> n2 Replicate(op=37, value=19, epoch=1)  DROPPED (link cut)
    951  client -> n2 Read(op=38)
    961  n2 -> client ReadOk(op=38, value=19)
    976  client -> n2 Write(op=39, value=20)
    978  n1 -> n2 Replicate(op=37, value=19, epoch=1)  DROPPED (link cut)
    979  n1 -> n2 Replicate(op=37, value=19, epoch=1)  DROPPED (link cut)
    984  link n1-n2 healed
    984  n2 -> client Ack(op=39)
    996  client -> n2 Read(op=40)
   1005  n2 -> client ReadOk(op=40, value=20)
   1013  n1 -> n2 Replicate(op=37, value=19, epoch=1)
   1013  VIOLATION: at 1013 ms n2 is the primary and holds 19, but write 20 was acknowledged

Replaying seed 4: 190 trace lines, identical to the first run: true

The fixed protocol (epochs) on the same 10,000 seeds: 0 failures.
That was 15,000 simulated seconds in 3,507 ms of real time.
```

Seeds 0 to 3 pass and seed 4 fails: the link between n1 and n2 is cut for 175 ms, n2 promotes itself, and when the link heals, n1's resend of write 19 (a write it accepted during the cut and never got confirmed) overwrites n2's 20. The replay is identical event for event, which is what makes a seed a bug report. The real time on the last line depends on your machine (a few seconds on a laptop); the simulated time doesn't.

sections.h: Model checking the design: TLA+ and P
sections.body:
The explorer you wrote in the last lesson is a model checker: given a model (states and the steps between them) and a rule, it visits every reachable state and returns a shortest trace that breaks the rule. **TLA+**, Leslie Lamport's specification language, is the industrial version. You describe the design as variables, an initial state and actions, where each action says how one step may change the variables. TLC, the TLA+ model checker, explores every reachable state of a bounded instance, say 3 nodes and at most 2 crashes, and checks your invariants in each. The election from the last lesson, starting from the state where both candidates have voted for themselves, looks like this:

```text
\* a sketch of two actions and the rule, not a complete spec
Vote(v, c) ==                               \* node v votes for candidate c
    /\ up[v] /\ votedFor[v] = Nil
    /\ votedFor' = [votedFor EXCEPT ![v] = c]
    /\ votes' = [votes EXCEPT ![c] = @ \cup {v}]
    /\ UNCHANGED up

Restart(v) ==                               \* crash-recovery, vote kept in memory
    /\ votedFor' = [votedFor EXCEPT ![v] = Nil]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<up, votes>>

OneLeader == \A a, b \in Candidates :
    Cardinality(votes[a]) >= 2 /\ Cardinality(votes[b]) >= 2 => a = b
```

Each action is a condition on the current state (unprimed variables) and the next one (primed). TLC would find the double vote in three steps: `Vote(n2, n1)`, `Restart(n2)`, `Vote(n2, n3)`.

Amazon's 2014 report is the best evidence that this pays outside academia. By then TLA+ had been used on 10 large systems, by 7 teams, and engineers from entry level to principal had learned it well enough for useful results in 2 to 3 weeks. The 939-line spec of DynamoDB's replication found the 35-step bug and two others. A fault-tolerant network algorithm in S3 (804 lines) had 2 bugs, and EBS volume management, only 102 lines, had 3. The teams also used specs to check optimizations they wouldn't otherwise have dared to make.

**P** is the other modelling language AWS uses: a system is a set of communicating state machines, and P's checker explores message interleavings and failures systematically. Its project page lists teams working on S3, EBS, DynamoDB, MemoryDB, Aurora, EC2 and IoT. PObserve checks logs from test and production runs against the P specification after the fact.

Model checking has two limits. The model is bounded, and the state space grows fast: the Try it shows the fixed election going from 268 states to 151,320 when it grows from 3 nodes and 1 crash to 5 nodes and 2. A bug that needs a bigger model or a longer run stays hidden. And the spec isn't the code: the design can be right while the Kotlin has a bug the spec doesn't, and the two drift apart as the code changes. PObserve exists to narrow that gap, and the next layer closes it from the other side.

try.title: Watch the state space grow
steps: Run the demo below. It explores the fixed election from the last lesson in full, for 3 and 5 nodes and up to 2 crashes.
Before it prints, guess how many states 5 nodes with 2 crashes have, given that 3 nodes with 1 crash have 268.
Which grows the state space faster here: one more crash, or two more nodes?
try.expect:
```text
The fixed election (votes on disk before replying), crash-recovery, explored in full:

nodes  crashes     states      time
    3        0         36     21 ms
    3        1        268      7 ms
    3        2        940      9 ms
    5        0      2,916     21 ms
    5        1     31,060    120 ms
    5        2    151,320    501 ms
```

Two more nodes multiply the states by 80 to 160; one more crash multiplies them by 3.5 to 11. Every extra node adds messages that can arrive in any order. The times are small and vary with JIT warm-up (the first row includes it). Real specifications hit the same wall sooner, which is why Amazon ran TLC distributed across ten EC2 instances for the DynamoDB spec, and why every model is bounded.

sections.h: Deterministic simulation: the real code in a fake world
sections.body:
Deterministic simulation testing (DST) runs the real code, many times, in a world the test controls. Everything that could differ between two runs goes through one seeded random number generator and one virtual clock: which message arrives next and when, which disk write fails, when a node crashes or pauses, what the clock reads. Nothing sleeps; the clock jumps to the next event. A run is then a pure function of its seed. Search seed after seed, check the invariants after every event, and when one fails, the seed is a complete bug report: run it again and the same thing happens at the same simulated millisecond, under a debugger if you like.

The lab builds a small one. Two nodes replicate one register: the primary applies a write, waits for the backup's confirmation, then acknowledges the client, and a backup that hears nothing for 100 ms promotes itself. The simulator's model allows message delays of 1 to 10 ms and one fault per run on n1: a pause, a cut link or a crash. It finds a lost write at seed 4. The stepper shows seed 36: n1 pauses for 172 ms, n2 promotes itself and acknowledges write 10, then n1 wakes still believing it's primary, and its late copy of write 9 overwrites n2's 10. Crashes alone never trigger it. The fix is lesson 5's fencing token: an epoch that the new primary raises and the old one can't match.

FoundationDB was built this way from its first line. All of its nondeterminism (network, disk, time, random numbers) sits behind interfaces, so many FoundationDB servers and the test workload run inside one single-threaded discrete-event simulator. Besides machine, rack and network faults, the code cooperates through **buggification**: at chosen points it may return an unusual error, add a delay or pick an odd tuning value, so rare paths run often. Because the simulated clock skips idle time, bugs that take a long time to unfold show up fast. Apple's CloudKit has run FoundationDB for more than 0.5 million disk-years without a data corruption event. TigerBeetle's simulator, the VOPR, runs a cluster of real TigerBeetle code under network, storage and process faults at 1000 times real speed, around the clock on 1,024 cores. Antithesis works a level lower: its deterministic hypervisor runs ordinary containers on one CPU core with a virtual clock, so software never written for simulation becomes reproducible.

The price is fidelity. The FoundationDB paper names the limits: simulation can't find performance problems, can't test third-party libraries or code outside its framework, and can't catch an operating system or file system that behaves differently from what the simulator assumes.

stepper.title: A paused primary comes back as a zombie
stepper.intro: Seed 36 from the lab's simulator, naive protocol: a pause of n1 at 340 ms for 172 ms. The last frame replays it with epochs.

frames.say: Normal running, up to 340 ms. The client sends write 9 to n1, the primary. n1 applies it, replicates it to n2, and will acknowledge only once n2 confirms. n2 has applied 9 and sent its confirmation back.

frames.say: At 340 ms n1 stops: a long GC pause or a VM stall, as in lesson 4 of this track. n2's confirmation of write 9 waits in its inbox, and so do two resends of write 9 from the client, which got no acknowledgement within 50 ms.

frames.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 680 296" role="img" aria-label="At 440 ms n2 has heard nothing for 100 ms, promotes itself and points the registry at itself."><defs><marker id="arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" class="ln"/></marker></defs><text class="t t-a" x="20" y="36" text-anchor="start">t = 440 ms</text><rect class="box-a" x="265" y="14" width="150" height="56" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="340" y="37" text-anchor="middle">client</text><text class="t-s t-a" x="340" y="57" text-anchor="middle">registry: n2</text><rect class="box-bad" x="20" y="150" width="210" height="100" rx="8"/><text class="t t-bad" x="125" y="174" text-anchor="middle">n1</text><text class="t-s" x="125" y="196" text-anchor="middle">PAUSED until 512 ms</text><text class="t-s" x="125" y="216" text-anchor="middle">value 9</text><text class="t-s" x="125" y="236" text-anchor="middle">inbox: ok, write 9 x2</text><rect class="box-a" x="450" y="150" width="210" height="100" rx="8"/><text class="t t-a" x="555" y="174" text-anchor="middle">n2</text><text class="t-s" x="555" y="196" text-anchor="middle">primary, alone</text><text class="t-s" x="555" y="216" text-anchor="middle">value 9</text><text class="t-s" x="555" y="236" text-anchor="middle">promoted itself</text></svg>
frames.say: At 440 ms n2 has heard nothing from n1 for 100 ms. It promotes itself, tells the registry, and from now on acknowledges writes alone, because as far as it can tell n1 is dead.

frames.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 680 296" role="img" aria-label="The client resends write 9 to n2, which acknowledges it; then a read returns 9 and write 10 is acknowledged."><defs><marker id="arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" class="ln"/></marker></defs><text class="t t-a" x="20" y="36" text-anchor="start">t = 472 to 515 ms</text><rect class="box" x="265" y="14" width="150" height="56" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="340" y="37" text-anchor="middle">client</text><text class="t-s" x="340" y="57" text-anchor="middle">registry: n2</text><rect class="box-bad" x="20" y="150" width="210" height="100" rx="8"/><text class="t t-bad" x="125" y="174" text-anchor="middle">n1</text><text class="t-s" x="125" y="196" text-anchor="middle">PAUSED until 512 ms</text><text class="t-s" x="125" y="216" text-anchor="middle">value 9</text><text class="t-s" x="125" y="236" text-anchor="middle">inbox: ok, write 9 x2</text><rect class="box-a" x="450" y="150" width="210" height="100" rx="8"/><text class="t t-a" x="555" y="174" text-anchor="middle">n2</text><text class="t-s" x="555" y="196" text-anchor="middle">primary, alone</text><text class="t-s" x="555" y="216" text-anchor="middle">value 10</text><text class="t-s" x="555" y="236" text-anchor="middle">acked write 10 at 515</text><line class="ln-a" x1="390" y1="72" x2="528" y2="148" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><text class="t-s" x="475" y="109" text-anchor="start">write 9, read, write 10</text></svg>
frames.say: The client's next resend goes to n2. Write 9 is acknowledged at 481 ms, a read returns 9, and write 10 is acknowledged at 515 ms. Every acknowledged write is on n2.

frames.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 680 296" role="img" aria-label="n1 wakes at 512 ms, still believing it is primary, applies the queued write 9 and replicates it to n2."><defs><marker id="arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" class="ln"/></marker></defs><text class="t t-a" x="20" y="36" text-anchor="start">t = 512 ms</text><rect class="box" x="265" y="14" width="150" height="56" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="340" y="37" text-anchor="middle">client</text><text class="t-s" x="340" y="57" text-anchor="middle">registry: n2</text><rect class="box-a" x="20" y="150" width="210" height="100" rx="8"/><text class="t t-a" x="125" y="174" text-anchor="middle">n1</text><text class="t-s" x="125" y="196" text-anchor="middle">awake, still primary</text><text class="t-s" x="125" y="216" text-anchor="middle">value 9</text><text class="t-s" x="125" y="236" text-anchor="middle">works through inbox</text><rect class="box" x="450" y="150" width="210" height="100" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="555" y="174" text-anchor="middle">n2</text><text class="t-s" x="555" y="196" text-anchor="middle">primary, alone</text><text class="t-s" x="555" y="216" text-anchor="middle">value 10</text><text class="t-s" x="555" y="236" text-anchor="middle"></text><line class="ln-bad" x1="234" y1="200" x2="446" y2="200" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><text class="t-s t-bad" x="340" y="190" text-anchor="middle">replicate 9 (late)</text></svg>
frames.say: At 512 ms n1 wakes. Nothing told it that time passed, so it still believes it's primary. It handles its inbox in order: the old confirmation (it acknowledges write 9 a second time, harmlessly), then the two resends of write 9, which it applies and replicates to n2.

frames.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 680 296" role="img" aria-label="At 520 ms n2 applies the late replicate: its value falls from 10 to 9, so acknowledged write 10 is lost."><defs><marker id="arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" class="ln"/></marker></defs><text class="t t-a" x="20" y="36" text-anchor="start">t = 520 ms</text><rect class="box" x="265" y="14" width="150" height="56" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="340" y="37" text-anchor="middle">client</text><text class="t-s" x="340" y="57" text-anchor="middle">registry: n2</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="150" width="210" height="100" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="125" y="174" text-anchor="middle">n1</text><text class="t-s" x="125" y="196" text-anchor="middle">still primary</text><text class="t-s" x="125" y="216" text-anchor="middle">value 9</text><text class="t-s" x="125" y="236" text-anchor="middle"></text><rect class="box-bad" x="450" y="150" width="210" height="100" rx="8"/><text class="t t-bad" x="555" y="174" text-anchor="middle">n2</text><text class="t-s" x="555" y="196" text-anchor="middle">primary, alone</text><text class="t-s" x="555" y="216" text-anchor="middle">value 9</text><text class="t-s" x="555" y="236" text-anchor="middle">applied the late copy</text><text class="t-s t-bad" x="340" y="282" text-anchor="middle">VIOLATION: write 10 was acknowledged, the primary holds 9</text></svg>
frames.say: At 520 ms the late Replicate reaches n2, which applies it like any other. Its value goes back from 10 to 9: write 10 was acknowledged and is gone. The simulator's check fires on this exact event, and seed 36 replays it every time.

frames.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 680 296" role="img" aria-label="With the fix, n2 is in epoch 2, n1 steps down when it wakes, and n2 refuses n1's epoch-1 replicate."><defs><marker id="arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" class="ln"/></marker></defs><text class="t t-a" x="20" y="36" text-anchor="start">with epochs</text><rect class="box" x="265" y="14" width="150" height="56" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="340" y="37" text-anchor="middle">client</text><text class="t-s" x="340" y="57" text-anchor="middle">registry: n2</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="150" width="210" height="100" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="125" y="174" text-anchor="middle">n1</text><text class="t-s" x="125" y="196" text-anchor="middle">stepped down</text><text class="t-s" x="125" y="216" text-anchor="middle">epoch 2</text><text class="t-s" x="125" y="236" text-anchor="middle">its writes are refused</text><rect class="box-ok" x="450" y="150" width="210" height="100" rx="8"/><text class="t t-ok" x="555" y="174" text-anchor="middle">n2</text><text class="t-s" x="555" y="196" text-anchor="middle">primary, epoch 2</text><text class="t-s" x="555" y="216" text-anchor="middle">value 10</text><text class="t-s" x="555" y="236" text-anchor="middle">refuses epoch 1</text><line class="ln-d" x1="234" y1="200" x2="446" y2="200" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><text class="t-s" x="340" y="190" text-anchor="middle">replicate 9, epoch 1</text><text class="t-s t-ok" x="340" y="282" text-anchor="middle">same seed, same pause: n2 refuses epoch 1 and keeps 10</text></svg>
frames.say: The same seed and pause with the fix. n2 promoted itself into epoch 2, and the first of its heartbeats that n1 handles makes n1 step down. The Replicates n1 sent a moment earlier carry epoch 1, so n2 refuses them and keeps 10. This is lesson 5's fencing token, checked by the node that holds the data.

try.title: Replay seed 36
steps: Run the demo below twice. It prints the whole trace of seed 36 for the naive protocol, heartbeats left out.
Compare the two runs. Then find the event where the damage happens and the event that caused it 8 ms earlier.
Open `labs/sim/src/main/kotlin/sfz/dist/l08/Simulation.kt` and find every place randomness comes from. In the lab you'll find that one of them is wrong.
try.expect:
Both runs print the same lines. The part from the pause on (output trimmed):

```text
  340  n1 PAUSED until 512
  440  n2: heard nothing from n1 for 100 ms: promoting myself
  440  n2: registry: clients now go to n2
  472  client -> n2 Write(op=17, value=9)
  481  n2 -> client Ack(op=17)
  493  client -> n2 Read(op=18)
  495  n2 -> client ReadOk(op=18, value=9)
  506  client -> n2 Write(op=19, value=10)
  512  n2 -> n1 ReplicateOk(op=17, epoch=1)
  512  client -> n1 Write(op=17, value=9)
  512  client -> n1 Write(op=17, value=9)
  514  n1 -> client Ack(op=17)
  515  n2 -> client Ack(op=19)
  520  n1 -> n2 Replicate(op=17, value=9, epoch=1)
  520  VIOLATION: at 520 ms n2 is the primary and holds 9, but write 10 was acknowledged
```

The damage is at 520 ms, and its cause is n1 handling the client's queued resends at 512 ms, when it woke. Nothing in the trace depends on your machine: a different laptop, a slower CPU or a debugger attached all give the same 15 lines.

sections.body:
Simulation tests the code you can put in the simulator. **Jepsen**, Kyle Kingsbury's testing library and the analyses he publishes with it, tests the system you actually run: real binaries on real or virtual machines, over a real network, judged only by what clients saw. A test has four parts. A generator produces operations for many concurrent clients. A **nemesis** injects faults while they run: partitions made with firewall rules, killed and paused processes, clock changes, and writes lost because they were never fsynced (LazyFS, a file system that drops unsynced data on a simulated power failure). Every operation goes into a **history** twice, once when invoked and once when it completes as ok, fail, or info when the client doesn't know what happened (the timeout from lesson 1 of this track). Then a checker asks whether any order of those operations fits the guarantee the database claims.

Elle is the checker for transactions. Its list-append workload makes each write append a unique element to a list, so every read reveals the order of all the writes before it. From that, Elle infers which transaction must have come before which, and searches the graph for cycles: the anomalies of the Transactions track (G0, G1c, G-single, G2). It scales roughly linearly with history length; a 22-million-transaction history checks in about two minutes.

The results keep humbling well-tested systems. Jepsen's 2025 analysis of TigerBeetle 0.16.11, a database designed around its simulator, found two safety bugs (queries with several filters that omitted results, and a debugging API in the Java client that returned wrong timestamps) and seven crashes. Two crashes came from single-bit flips in padding and in a superblock field. The VOPR had missed them because it corrupted whole sectors: a corrupted sector fails its checksum and gets repaired, so the code that checks padding never ran. The query bug escaped four fuzzers because none of them produced the data that sends a join down its zig-zag path. A simulator finds only the faults its authors thought to inject and the workloads they thought to generate. Jepsen still credited TigerBeetle's simulation for much of the system's robustness, and reminded readers that such tests can prove the presence of bugs, not their absence. In March 2026 it reported lost updates on healthy MariaDB Galera Cluster 12.1.2 clusters.

A black-box checker sees only what clients observed. The lab's naive protocol loses a write in 1,559 of 10,000 runs, but a client read shows it in only 883. In the rest, a newer write covers the damage before anyone reads, or the client has already stopped. That is why Jepsen tests usually heal the network at the end and read everything back.

try.title: Check the client's history, not the servers
steps: Run the demo below. It runs the naive protocol on 10,000 seeds twice over: once judged by the simulator's check of both servers after every event, once by a Jepsen-style checker that sees only the client's history.
Predict which count is larger, and why they can differ at all.
In the history it prints, find the two acknowledged writes that were lost.
try.expect:
```text
Naive protocol, 10,000 seeds:
  runs that lost an acknowledged write (god's-eye check after every event): 1,559
  of those, runs where the client's own history shows it (a stale read):    883

Seed 10 (Cut(at=244, forMs=216)), the client's history around the first stale read:
   op  kind  value  invoked  completed  attempts
    9  write     5   188 ms     214 ms         1
   10  read      5   219 ms     230 ms         1
   11  write     6   235 ms     396 ms         4
   12  read      6   401 ms     416 ms         1
   13  write     7   421 ms     432 ms         1
   14  read      7   437 ms     450 ms         1
   15  write     8   455 ms     463 ms         1
   16  read      6   468 ms     478 ms         1
   17  write     9   483 ms     491 ms         1
  checker: read 16 returned 6 after write 8 was acknowledged
```

The god's-eye count is larger: 1,559 runs lost a write, and in 883 of them a later read showed it. Writes 7 and 8 were acknowledged, then read 16 returned 6, because n1's late copy of write 6 (the one that took 4 attempts during the cut) overwrote them. In the other 676 runs no read came between the damage and the next write, or the client had already stopped, so the history looks perfectly fine. Op 11's four attempts are the info outcomes a Jepsen history would record.

sections.h: Fault injection, chaos and property tests
sections.body:
The remaining layers are cheaper, and they catch more than their cost suggests.

**Fault injection** in ordinary integration tests puts a misbehaving network between your code and a real dependency. Toxiproxy is a TCP proxy for that, and Testcontainers ships it as a module (`org.testcontainers:testcontainers-toxiproxy:2.0.5`, image `ghcr.io/shopify/toxiproxy:2.5.0`). A test adds a toxic, such as 1,100 ms of latency on the response path or a bandwidth of 0 to cut the connection, and checks what your service does: does the timeout fire, does the retry carry the idempotency key, does the circuit breaker open? You choose one fault at a time, which is both its strength and its limit.

Chaos engineering runs experiments in production, on purpose. Netflix's Chaos Monkey, which terminated instances at random, made it famous, but the Principles of Chaos Engineering describe something more careful: define a measurable steady state (checkouts per minute, p99 authorization latency), predict that it holds in both a control group and an experimental group, introduce one real-world event, look for a difference, and keep the blast radius small. It is the only layer that tests your alerts, runbooks and people, and the wrong place to look for a lost write.

Property-based testing generates the inputs. You state a property, such as "no acknowledged write is ever lost", and the library tries hundreds of generated cases; when one fails, it shrinks it to a small one that still fails. In the lab, jqwik 1.10.2 generates the fault itself and shrinks a failure to something like "a pause of n1 at 100 ms for 133 ms", which reads as a bug report. Kotest's `kotest-property` module does the same in Kotlin with `checkAll`. It catches the bug the seed search found, from another direction: the search draws whole runs from a seed, while the generator knows what a fault looks like and can make it smaller.

No single method is enough. Each one checks something the others can't:

| Method | Checks | Misses |
|---|---|---|
| TLA+, P | the design, every schedule of a small model | bugs in the code; bugs that need a bigger model |
| Deterministic simulation | the real code, millions of replayable runs | faults and workloads nobody put in the simulator |
| Jepsen and Elle | the deployed system under real faults | what no client observes; it can't prove absence |
| Property-based tests | one component on generated inputs | interactions between components |
| Fault injection, chaos | your service and your operations under one real fault | rare combinations of faults |

try.title: Let jqwik shrink the bug
steps: Do this before you fix `PrimaryBackup` in the lab, while it is still the naive protocol. Run the property test below from the `labs` folder.
Read the failure. Which fault did jqwik shrink to, and how long is the pause compared with the 100 ms failover timeout?
Open `labs/sim/build/reports/tests/test/index.html`, find `NoLostWritePropertyTest` and read its standard output: jqwik prints the original failing sample next to the shrunk one.
try.expect:
Something like this; jqwik picks its own random cases, so your numbers will differ:

```text
NoLostWritePropertyTest > with your protocol no acknowledged write is ever lost FAILED
    org.opentest4j.AssertionFailedError: [seed 0, Pause(at=100, forMs=133)]
    expected: null
     but was: "at 245 ms n2 is the primary and holds 3, but write 4 was acknowledged"

NoLostWritePropertyTest > with your protocol no client ever reads a value older than one it saw acknowledged FAILED
    java.lang.AssertionError: [seed -30634, Pause(at=102, forMs=154)]
    Expecting empty but was: ["read 8 returned 3 after write 4 was acknowledged"]

2 tests completed, 2 failed
```

and in the report's standard output, for the first property (trimmed):

```text
Shrunk Sample (15 steps)
------------------------
  arg0: Pause(at=100, forMs=133)
  arg1: 0

Original Sample
---------------
  arg0: Cut(at=115, forMs=241)
  arg1: -4328077047102738090
```

The original failure was a 241 ms cut starting at 115 ms. jqwik shrank it to a pause at the earliest start it allows (100 ms) lasting 133 ms: just long enough for n2 to promote itself (100 ms) and acknowledge one more write before n1 wakes. The shrunk case is the bug report.

analogy: Testing a distributed system is like crash-testing cars. A model checker is the engineer's calculation: it covers every case on paper, for the car as drawn. Deterministic simulation is the crash lab, with the same real car hit from every angle at every speed, filmed so any crash can be replayed frame by frame. Jepsen is an independent safety agency that buys the car from a showroom and crashes it its own way. Property tests check single parts, a seat belt or an airbag, on a bench. Chaos engineering is a carefully supervised test drive in traffic. No carmaker skips the lab because it did the calculation. The analogy breaks on one point: a crash lab can only stage crashes someone imagined, and so can a simulator, while real roads, and real networks, keep inventing new ones.
in_your_world: You can start without a new tool. Wherever your Kotlin service decides something over time (a payment saga's retry policy, a lease renewer, an outbox relay), pass in `java.time.Clock` and a seeded `Random` instead of reading the system clock and `Random.Default`, and write the logic as a function of messages and timer events rather than threads and sleeps. Then the same code runs in production and in a simulator test that tries thousands of seeds. Temporal already holds you to this: workflow code must be deterministic, so its history can be replayed, which is the same discipline. Add Toxiproxy between the service and Oracle or the card issuer's sandbox in your Testcontainers tests to check timeouts and idempotent retries one fault at a time, and read the Jepsen analysis of anything you depend on before you trust its consistency claims: Kafka-compatible brokers, etcd clients and managed PostgreSQL all have one.
mistake: The common mistake is building a simulator that isn't deterministic and not noticing. A run reads `System.currentTimeMillis()` deep in a library, iterates a `HashSet` of objects that use identity hash codes, or lets a second thread race the event loop, and then a failing seed doesn't fail again on your machine. People don't notice because the first runs pass, so nobody tries to replay one. Test the simulator itself: run one seed twice and compare the whole trace, as the lab's first test does, on every build. The second mistake is the opposite: trusting a passing simulator too much. It only explores the faults you modelled. When Jepsen, an incident or a user finds a bug, first make the simulator reproduce it, the way FoundationDB reproduced field bugs in simulation before debugging them.

compare.title: What a black-box checker sees, against what the simulator knows

a.label: Jepsen's view: the client history
a.title: seed 10, from the client's side only
a.src:
op  kind  value  invoked  completed  attempts
13  write     7   421 ms     432 ms         1
14  read      7   437 ms     450 ms         1
15  write     8   455 ms     463 ms         1
16  read      6   468 ms     478 ms         1
checker: read 16 returned 6 after write 8 was acknowledged

b.label: The simulator's view: every event
b.title: seed 36, both servers and the network
b.src:
512  client -> n1 Write(op=17, value=9)
  514  n1 -> client Ack(op=17)
  515  n2 -> client Ack(op=19)
  520  n1 -> n2 Replicate(op=17, value=9, epoch=1)
  520  VIOLATION: at 520 ms n2 is the primary and holds 9,
       but write 10 was acknowledged

compare.note: The history on the left is all Jepsen ever has: what each client asked, what came back and when. From it, a checker can prove an anomaly happened (read 16 can't return 6 after write 8 was acknowledged) but not why, and it misses any damage no read observed. The trace on the right sees every message and both servers, so it catches the lost write at the event that caused it, and the seed replays it. The price of that view is that it exists only for code running inside the simulator, under the faults someone wrote into it.

worked.title: A deterministic simulator in five moves

steps.say: Route every random choice through one generator made from the seed. Draw the fault first, even when the test passes one in, so the delays that follow come out the same either way.
Replace time with a queue of events ordered by virtual time, then by the order they were scheduled, so two events at the same millisecond always run in the same order.
Make faults decisions of the event loop. A crashed node's events are dropped; a paused node's events wait until it wakes, in their original order.
steps.code:
val e = queue.poll()
now = e.at
if (e.node != null && e.node in down) continue          // crashed: does nothing
val wake = e.node?.let { pausedUntil[it] }
if (wake != null && now < wake) { schedule(wake, e.node, e.action); continue }  // paused: later
e.action()

steps.say: Check the invariant after every event, with the god's-eye view a real test never has.
steps.code:
val primary = servers.getValue(registry)
if (primary.value < highestAcked) violation = "at $now ms ${primary.name} holds ${primary.value}, but write $highestAcked was acknowledged"

steps.say: Search seeds and keep the first failure. Replaying it is just running the same seed again.

lab.title: A seeded simulator that catches a zombie primary
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. All 8 fail: 6 in `SimulationTest` and 2 jqwik properties in `NoLostWritePropertyTest`. If you haven't done the last Try it yet, read the jqwik failure now: it is the naive protocol's bug, already shrunk.

Read `Simulation.kt` from the top. It is finished apart from one line: the event queue, the network, the faults, the client and the god's-eye check are given. Read `NaivePrimaryBackup` in `PrimaryBackup.kt` too, and find the line marked as the bug.
In `Dst.kt`, write `search` (exercise 1). Run `--tests 'sfz.dist.l08.SimulationTest'`: the search finds a failing seed, but the tests that replay a seed still fail.
Exercise 2: one line in `Simulation.kt` draws a random number without the seed. Find it and fix it. The replay tests pass.
Exercise 3: give `PrimaryBackup` epochs, as its KDoc describes. Run all 8 tests. The fixed protocol must survive 2,000 seeds and 600 jqwik-generated faults.
hints: `search` is a `for` loop over `seeds` that returns the first `Simulation(seed, protocol, faultFor?.invoke(seed)).run()` whose `violation` isn't null.
Exercise 2: look at how `send` picks a delay. `Random.nextLong` is `Random.Default`, seeded differently in every JVM; the simulation's own generator is `rng`.

Exercise 3: write one helper, `admit(theirs: Int): Boolean`, for every message from the peer: answer `Refused(epoch)` and return false if `theirs < epoch`; adopt `theirs` and step down if it is larger; then set `lastHeard` and return true.
Promotion is `epoch += 1` next to `isPrimary = true`. Every `Replicate` and `Heartbeat` sends `epoch`, and stepping down clears `waiting` so the old primary never acknowledges those writes.
If `a deposed primary steps down` fails, check that your step-down calls `env.log` with the words `steps down`.

drill.title: Write the simulator's loop from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the main loop of a discrete-event simulator: events ordered by time and then by scheduling order; skip events for crashed nodes; push a paused node's events to its wake-up time; run the event and check the invariant. Then name two things that would make two runs of the same seed differ.

recap: Distributed bugs hide in rare schedules: Amazon's DynamoDB bug needed 35 steps, and 88% of studied partition failures needed only one isolated node. Ordinary tests sample a few schedules and can't replay them.
TLA+ and P check the design in every schedule of a bounded model (AWS: 10 systems, 7 teams, learned in 2 to 3 weeks). They miss bugs in the code and bugs that need a bigger model.
Deterministic simulation runs the real code with every random choice from one seed and a virtual clock, so a failing seed replays exactly (FoundationDB, TigerBeetle's VOPR, Antithesis).
A simulator finds only the faults and workloads it was given: Jepsen found TigerBeetle bugs from single-bit flips the VOPR never injected.
Jepsen judges the deployed system by its client history (invoke, then ok, fail or info), with Elle finding dependency cycles. It can prove bugs exist, never that none do.
Toxiproxy tests your code against one real fault, chaos experiments test production and its people, and property tests (jqwik, Kotest) shrink failures to a minimal case. Use several layers.

quiz.q: TigerBeetle's simulator runs around the clock on 1,024 cores, yet Jepsen found a crash caused by a single flipped bit in padding. Why had the simulator missed it?
options: The simulator ran too few seeds to reach that schedule
It corrupted whole sectors, which fail their checksum and get repaired, so the code that checks padding never ran
Simulation can't model disks at all
The bug was only in the Java client, which the simulator doesn't run
quiz.why: The VOPR's fault model corrupted whole sectors. A corrupted sector fails its checksum, TigerBeetle repairs it from another replica, and the padding check behind the checksum is never reached. More seeds wouldn't help, because no seed produced that fault; TigerBeetle fixed it by teaching the simulator to flip single bytes. Simulators model disks fine, and this crash was in the server.

quiz.q: A TLA+ model of your failover passes TLC with 3 nodes and at most 2 crashes. What has that shown?
options: Your Kotlin implementation of the failover is correct
The design is correct for any number of nodes
Nothing, since model checking only finds syntax errors in specs
The design keeps its invariants in every schedule of that bounded model
quiz.why: TLC explored every reachable state of the model you gave it: 3 nodes, up to 2 crashes. Inside those bounds no schedule breaks your invariants, which is strong evidence about the design. It says nothing about whether the Kotlin matches the spec, and a bug that needs 5 nodes or a third crash is outside the model. That gap is what simulation and Jepsen-style testing are for.

quiz.q: Your simulation test fails on CI for seed 48213, but the same seed passes on your laptop. What is the most likely cause?
options: Something in the code takes randomness or time from outside the seed: the wall clock, `Random.Default`, a `HashSet` ordered by identity hash codes, or a second thread
The seed is too large for the random number generator
The JIT compiles the code differently on CI
The simulator needs more memory on your laptop
quiz.why: A run of a deterministic simulator is a function of its seed, so a seed that behaves differently on two machines means something nondeterministic got in. The usual suspects are a real clock read, an unseeded generator, iteration order that depends on identity hash codes, and real threads. JIT compilation changes speed, not results, and any `Long` is a valid seed. The lab's first test exists to catch this.

quiz.q: From lesson 7: the lab's simulator allows at most one fault per run, always on n1. The fixed protocol passes 10,000 seeds. A teammate wants to call it correct. What can you claim?
options: It is correct under any faults, since 10,000 runs is a lot
Nothing, because simulations can't show anything
It kept every acknowledged write in every one of those runs, which is evidence inside that fault model only; two faults, or a fault on n2, are outside it
It is correct as long as the network never partitions
quiz.why: A simulator's fault model is its system model, and a passing search, like a proof, says nothing outside it. Inside, 10,000 seeds with cuts, pauses and crashes is real evidence. But the protocol was never tried with n1 pausing and then losing its link, or with n2 failing while it runs alone, so you can't claim those. The last option is wrong twice: cuts are in the model, and passing them is part of the evidence.

quiz.q: What makes a chaos experiment different from killing random pods?
options: Chaos experiments only run in staging
It starts from a hypothesis about a measurable steady state, introduces one real-world event against a control group, and keeps the blast radius small
Chaos experiments replay a recorded seed, like a simulator
Killing pods is chaos engineering; the difference is only in the tooling
quiz.why: The Principles of Chaos Engineering describe an experiment: define steady state (say checkouts per minute), predict it holds in both a control and an experimental group, vary one real-world event, look for a difference, and limit the damage. Random kills without a hypothesis tell you little. The principles explicitly favour running in production, and nothing in production replays from a seed.

flashcards.front: What are the outcomes of an operation in a Jepsen history?
flashcards.back: Each operation is recorded when invoked and when it completes: ok (it happened), fail (it definitely didn't), or info (the client doesn't know, as after a timeout).

flashcards.front: What does Elle do, in one line?
flashcards.back: From a history of transactions (best with list-append), it infers which transaction must precede which and searches the graph for cycles, the isolation anomalies G0, G1c, G-single and G2.

flashcards.front: What does TLC do with a TLA+ spec?
flashcards.back: It explores every reachable state of a bounded instance of the spec and checks the invariants in each, reporting a shortest trace to any violation.

flashcards.front: What must be true for a simulation run to be a function of its seed?
flashcards.back: Every source of nondeterminism goes through the seeded generator and the virtual clock: message order and delay, faults, time, randomness. No real clocks, no unseeded random numbers, no real threads.
FoundationDB's technique of letting the simulator make the code itself misbehave at chosen points (an unusual error, a delay, an odd tuning value) so rare paths run often.

flashcards.front: Why can a simulator that ran for years still miss a bug Jepsen finds?
flashcards.back: It only injects the faults its authors modelled and generates the workloads they wrote. TigerBeetle's VOPR corrupted whole sectors, never single bits, so a padding check never ran.

flashcards.front: What does shrinking give you in a property-based test?
flashcards.back: When a generated case fails, the library tries smaller versions and reports the smallest that still fails, such as one pause of 133 ms at 100 ms, which reads as a bug report.

terms.plain: Visiting every reachable state of a bounded model of a design and checking rules in each.
Leslie Lamport's language for specifying designs as states and actions; TLC is its model checker.
Running real code many times with all randomness and time controlled by a seed, so any failing run replays exactly.
Making code misbehave on purpose at chosen points during simulation, so rare paths get exercised.
The part of a Jepsen test that injects faults: partitions, kills, pauses, clock changes, lost unsynced writes.
Jepsen's checker that finds transaction isolation anomalies as cycles in a dependency graph inferred from a history.
Stating a rule and letting a library generate many inputs, shrinking any failure to a minimal case.
Controlled experiments in production that test a hypothesis about steady-state behaviour under a real fault.

explain_back.prompt: Your team is building a ledger replicated with Raft, and someone asks which testing to invest in. Explain what each layer would catch and why you'd want more than one.
explain_back.answer: Start with the design: a TLA+ or P model of our replication and failover, checked on 3 nodes with a couple of crashes, catches design bugs like a vote that isn't durable or a failover that loses acknowledged entries, in every schedule of that small model. It can't see bugs in our Kotlin. For that, write the node logic against an injected clock, a seeded random generator and a fake network, and run it in a deterministic simulator: thousands of seeded runs with crashes, pauses and partitions, invariants checked after every event, and any failure replays from its seed. The simulator only finds faults we modelled, so before we trust the deployed system, run Jepsen-style tests against real binaries: partitions, kills, power loss with unsynced writes, judged by the client history with a checker such as Elle. Property tests cover components like the log codec, Toxiproxy in integration tests checks our timeouts and idempotent retries, and chaos experiments in production check alerts and runbooks. Each layer misses something the others catch, so a pass at one tells us nothing about the rest.

deeper.body:
**Determinism at three levels.** FoundationDB and TigerBeetle get determinism from how the application is written: one event loop, every outside effect behind an interface. Other projects get it from the runtime, replacing the scheduler or the async runtime under unchanged code. Antithesis gets it from the machine, with a hypervisor that makes a whole set of containers deterministic. The trade is effort against fidelity: the higher the level, the less of the real world the simulation sees, and the lower, the slower each run.

**On the JVM.** `kotlinx-coroutines-test`'s `runTest` already runs coroutines on a virtual clock that skips `delay`, so a test of a suspend function that waits 30 seconds finishes at once. It isn't a seeded scheduler that explores interleavings, but it removes real sleeps, which is the first step. The lab's simulator goes further with plain callbacks and one `PriorityQueue`.

**Swarm testing.** FoundationDB randomizes not only faults but the whole test: cluster size, configuration, workload, fault rates, and which buggification points are on. Runs that are each less thorough but differ from each other find more bugs than many runs of one carefully tuned configuration.

**Linearizability checking is hard.** Jepsen's older checker, Knossos, searches for an order of operations that matches a single-copy register, and that search grows exponentially with concurrency, which limits it to a few hundred operations. Elle avoids the search by choosing workloads whose reads reveal the order directly, at the cost of not being complete.

The framing of this lesson (formal methods, fault injection and deterministic simulation as complementary) follows Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 9. The lab's primary-backup protocol and its numbers are this course's own.
